headline.text: Internal funding is solid, but commitments are much larger

headline.text: Compute investment is accelerating ahead of delivered domestic capacity

summary.text: Information-processing investment grew 15.9%, while computer output rose 9.2% and semiconductor output rose 11.5%.
Announced domestic projects cover all 4 tracked critical supply-chain layers, but their $362.0B expected investment remains a commitment rather than operating capacity.
Semiconductor utilization at 72.2%, below computer utilization at 81.7%, suggests current production conditions differ across layers.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether announced projects progress as semiconductor utilization moves from 72.2%.

headline.text: The development pipeline is vast but poorly measured

summary.text: Available records show 1,556 development sites versus 3,068 operating sites, with published development capacity of 287.2 GW versus 22.9 GW for operating sites.
Because only 37.9% of active campus records have canonical published capacity, disclosed scale is substantial but incomplete and does not represent energized load.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether canonical capacity coverage rises from 37.9% and development sites shift into the operating count.

headline.text: National connectivity depth masks local interconnection gaps

summary.text: The public footprint includes 168 active U.S. IXPs, 90 international submarine cable systems and at least 250 interconnection facilities.
However, only 40 of 75 assessed population centers over 300k have an IXP, and 22 states combine data-center development with limited visible public interconnection depth.
The national backbone therefore does not establish campus-level connectivity readiness.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether the 22-state limited-depth count falls as federally supported middle-mile fiber expands.

headline.text: Planned supply does not yet resolve the large-load challenge

summary.text: Net planned generation additions total 227.0 GW through 2030, while published large-load campus records carry 263,644 MW of capacity.
Commercial electricity demand grew 2.9%, faster than total retail demand at 1.2%, while retail prices rose 5.4%.
The balance depends on planned additions becoming available rather than remaining pipeline capacity.

watchpoint.text: Watch changes in net planned generation against published large-load campus capacity through 2030.

headline.text: Queue scale overstates near-term grid availability

summary.text: The active queue totals 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages.
Historical delivery is weak: 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation, 75% withdrew, and 2025 completions took a median 5.0 years from request to commercial operation.
Storage adds 552.7 GW of queue interest, but its 2.8-hour operating weighted duration does not remove interconnection constraints.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether the 24.2% advanced share rises and median completion time falls from 5.0 years.

headline.text: Water exposure is visible, but facility use is largely undisclosed

summary.text: Only 63 of 1,906 mapped facilities have direct water evidence, and none has quantified withdrawal or consumption records.
Meanwhile, 239.2 GW of published data-center capacity lies in mapped states with some D2-or-worse drought area, including 81.0 GW where at least 25% of the state is affected.
This overlap identifies disclosure and screening needs, not campus-level water scarcity.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether quantified facility-use records rise above 0 and direct evidence expands beyond 3.3%.

headline.text: Consumer AI use remains far ahead of business deployment

summary.text: Among adults age 18–64, 61.8% report some generative-AI use and 45.2% report use for work, versus 21.5% of businesses reporting current AI use.
Expected business use within six months is 24.3%, only 2.8 percentage points above current use, indicating modest stated near-term expansion.
Large paid user counts show commercial traction but are not national adoption rates.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether current business use closes the 2.8-point gap with six-month expected use.

headline.text: Task exposure is broad while employment momentum is narrow

summary.text: Only 1 tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth; power and communication construction leads at 0.8%, while computing infrastructure trails at -4.1%.
The static benchmark finds median software-adjusted LLM task exposure of 45.8%, with 47.3% of occupations at or above 50% exposure.
That exposure signals potential task change, not measured job loss.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether positive employment breadth expands beyond 1 tracked channel or computing-infrastructure growth improves from -4.1%.

headline.text: Investment and provider growth outpace broad worker gains

summary.text: Information-processing investment grew 15.9%, while nonfarm-business productivity rose 2.2% and real hourly compensation rose 0.6%.
Since 2020, productivity increased 14.1% versus 4.5% for real hourly compensation, a 9.6-percentage-point gap, while the labor-share index declined 8.4%.
Strong provider revenue measures coexist with economy-wide gains, but they do not identify AI as their cause or establish broad returns.

watchpoint.text: Watch whether real compensation growth narrows the productivity gap and the labor-share index stops declining.

headline.text: Capital commitments are outrunning power delivery and realized business adoption

summary.text: Operating cash flow covers current CapEx by 1.46x, but forward commitments equal 5.16x current CapEx, placing expansion well beyond today’s internal funding coverage.
The buildout also faces a delivery test: 227.0 GW of planned generation through 2030 must move beyond pipeline status while published large-load campus records carry 263,644 MW.

At the use stage, 21.5% of businesses report current AI use, and expected use within six months is only 2.8 percentage points higher, leaving deployment narrower than the capital and infrastructure push.

watchpoint.text: Planned generation entering service alongside stronger business adoption would shift the thesis from commitment-led expansion toward delivered capacity and realized use.
